title: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The characteristic polynomial of an $n\times n$ matrix A is defined as $p_{A}(\lambda )=\det(\lambda I_{n}-A)$ , where det is the determinant operation, λ is a variable scalar element of the base ring, and In is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. Since each entry of the matrix $(\lambda I_{n}-A)$ is either constant or linear in λ, the determinant of $(\lambda I_{n}-A)$ is a degree-n monic polynomial in λ, so it can be written as $p_{A}(\lambda )=\lambda ^{n}+c_{n-1}\lambda ^{n-1}+\cdots +c_{1}\lambda +c_{0}.$ By replacing the scalar variable λ with the matrix A, one can define an analogous matrix polynomial expression, $p_{A}(A)=A^{n}+c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots +c_{1}A+c_{0}I_{n}.$ (Here, $A$ is the given matrix—not a variable, unlike $\lambda $ —so $p_{A}(A)$ is a constant rather than a function.) The Cayley–Hamilton theorem states that this polynomial expression is equal to the zero matrix, which is to say that $p_{A}(A)=0;$ that is, the characteristic polynomial $p_{A}$ is an annihilating polynomial for $A.$

title: Cellular approximation theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In algebraic topology, the cellular approximation theorem states that a map between CW-complexes can always be taken to be of a specific type. Concretely, if X and Y are CW-complexes, and f : X → Y is a continuous map, then f is said to be cellular if f takes the n-skeleton of X to the n-skeleton of Y for all n, i.e. if $f(X^{n})\subseteq Y^{n}$ for all n. The cellular approximation theorem states that any continuous map f : X → Y between CW-complexes X and Y is homotopic to a cellular map, and if f is already cellular on a subcomplex A of X, then we can furthermore choose the homotopy to be stationary on A. From an algebraic topological viewpoint, any map between CW-complexes can thus be taken to be cellular.

title: Cobham's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Cobham's theorem is a theorem in combinatorics on words that has important connections with number theory, notably transcendental numbers, and automata theory. Informally, the theorem gives the condition for the members of a set S of natural numbers written in bases b1 and base b2 to be recognised by finite automata. Specifically, consider bases b1 and b2 such that they are not powers of the same integer. Cobham's theorem states that S written in bases b1 and b2 is recognised by finite automata if and only if S differs by a finite set from a finite union of arithmetic progressions. title: De Bruijn–Erdős theorem (graph theory)

The De Bruijn–Erdős theorem concerns the chromatic numbers of infinite graphs, and shows that (again, assuming the axiom of choice) they can be calculated from the chromatic numbers of their finite subgraphs. It states that, if the chromatic numbers of the finite subgraphs of a graph $G$ have a finite maximum value $c$ , then the chromatic number of $G$ itself is exactly $c$ . On the other hand, if there is no finite upper bound on the chromatic numbers of the finite subgraphs of $G$ , then the chromatic number of $G$ itself must be infinite.

title: Deduction theorem

Deduction theorems exist for both propositional logic and first-order logic. statement: An economy has complete competitive markets, perfect information, price-taking agents and no externalities, and is at a competitive equilibrium. Its equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient.
hypotheses: An economy has complete competitive markets, perfect information, price-taking agents and no externalities, and is at a competitive equilibrium.
conclusions: Its equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient.

title: Gale–Ryser theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Each sequence can also be considered as an integer partition of the same number $m=\sum _{i=1}^{n}a_{i}$ . It turns out that partition $(a_{1}^{*},\ldots ,a_{n}^{*})$ where $a_{k}^{*}:=|\{b_{i}\mid b_{i}\geq k\}|$ is the conjugate partition of $(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{n})$ . The conjugate partition can be determined by a Ferrers diagram. Moreover, there is a connection to the relation majorization. Consider sequences $(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{n})$ , $(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{n})$ and $(a_{1}^{*},\ldots ,a_{n}^{*})$ as $n$ -dimensional vectors $a$ , $b$ and $a^{*}$ . Since $\sum _{i=1}^{k}a_{i}^{*}=\sum _{i=1}^{n}\min(b_{i},k)$ , the theorem above states that a pair of nonnegative integer sequences a and b with nonincreasing a is bigraphic if and only if the conjugate partition $b^{*}$ of $b$ majorizes $a$ .
statement: $a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_n$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ are sequences of nonnegative integers. They are the two degree sequences of some finite simple bipartite graph if and only if $\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\le\sum_{j=1}^m\min(b_j,k)$ for every $1\le k\le n$.
hypotheses: $a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_n$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ are sequences of nonnegative integers.
conclusions: They are the two degree sequences of some finite simple bipartite graph if and only if $\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\le\sum_{j=1}^m\min(b_j,k)$ for every $1\le k\le n$.

title: Gauss–Markov theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Suppose we have, in matrix notation, the linear relationship $y=X\beta +\varepsilon ,\quad (y,\varepsilon \in \mathbb {R} ^{n},\beta \in \mathbb {R} ^{K}{\text{ and }}X\in \mathbb {R} ^{n\times K}),$ where $\beta _{j}$ are non-random but unobservable parameters, $X_{ij}$ are non-random and observable (called the "explanatory variables"), $\varepsilon _{i}$ are random, and so $y_{i}$ are random. The random variables $\varepsilon _{i}$ are called the "disturbance", "noise" or simply "error" (will be contrasted with "residual" later in the article; see errors and residuals in statistics). Note that to include a constant in the model above, one can choose to introduce the constant as a variable $\beta _{K+1}$ with a newly introduced last column of $X$ being unity i.e., $X_{i(K+1)}=1$ for all $i$ . Note that though $y_{i}$ , as sample responses, are observable, the following statements and arguments including assumptions, proofs and the others assume under the only condition of knowing $X_{ij},$ but not $y_{i}.$
statement: The linear regression model has a full-rank design matrix, mean-zero errors with equal finite variance and mutually uncorrelated errors. The ordinary least-squares estimator is the best linear unbiased estimator of the regression coefficients: no other linear unbiased estimator has a smaller covariance matrix in the positive-semidefinite order.
hypotheses: The linear regression model has a full-rank design matrix, mean-zero errors with equal finite variance and mutually uncorrelated errors.
conclusions: The ordinary least-squares estimator is the best linear unbiased estimator of the regression coefficients: no other linear unbiased estimator has a smaller covariance matrix in the positive-semidefinite order.

title: Geiringer–Laman theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Geiringer-Laman Theorem. A graph $G=(V,E)$ is generically rigid in $2$ -dimensions with respect to bar-joint frameworks if and only if $G$ has a spanning subgraph $G'=(V,E')$ such that
statement: $G=(V,E)$ is a finite simple graph with at least two vertices. $G$ is generically rigid as a planar bar-joint framework if and only if it has a spanning edge subset $E'\subseteq E$ with $|E'|=2|V|-3$ and $|F|\le2|V(F)|-3$ for every nonempty $F\subseteq E'$.
hypotheses: $G=(V,E)$ is a finite simple graph with at least two vertices.
conclusions: $G$ is generically rigid as a planar bar-joint framework if and only if it has a spanning edge subset $E'\subseteq E$ with $|E'|=2|V|-3$ and $|F|\le2|V(F)|-3$ for every nonempty $F\subseteq E'$.

title: Gershgorin circle theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $D(a_{ii},R_{i})\subseteq \mathbb {C} $ be a closed disc centered at $a_{ii}$ with radius $R_{i}$ . Such a disc is called a Gershgorin disc.
statement: $A=(a_{ij})$ is a complex $n\times n$ matrix, and $D_i=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-a_{ii}|\le\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|\}$. Every eigenvalue of $A$ belongs to at least one Gershgorin disk $D_i$.

conclusions: Every eigenvalue of $A$ belongs to at least one Gershgorin disk $D_i$.

title: Goodman's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $M(K_{3},n)$ be the minimum number of unlabeled monochromatic copies of $K_{3}$ among all red–blue edge-colorings of $K_{n}$ . Goodman's theorem states that
statement: $n\ge1$ is an integer, and the edges of the complete graph $K_n$ are colored red or blue. The minimum possible number $M(K_3,n)$ of monochromatic triangles is $n(n-2)(n-4)/24$ if $n$ is even, $n(n-1)(n-5)/24$ if $n\equiv1\pmod4$, and $(n+1)(n-3)(n-4)/24$ if $n\equiv3\pmod4$.
hypotheses: $n\ge1$ is an integer, and the edges of the complete graph $K_n$ are colored red or blue.
conclusions: The minimum possible number $M(K_3,n)$ of monochromatic triangles is $n(n-2)(n-4)/24$ if $n$ is even, $n(n-1)(n-5)/24$ if $n\equiv1\pmod4$, and $(n+1)(n-3)(n-4)/24$ if $n\equiv3\pmod4$.

title: Grönwall's inequality
source_statement_excerpt: Let $I$ denote an interval of the real line of the form $[a,\infty )$ or $[a,b]$ or $[a,b)$ with $a<b$ . Let $\beta $ and $u$ be real-valued continuous functions defined on $I$ . If $u$ is differentiable in the interior $I^{\circ }$ of $I$ (the interval $I$ without the end points $a$ and possibly $b$ ) and satisfies the differential inequality
statement: $I$ is an interval beginning at $a$, $u,\beta$ are continuous on $I$, $u$ is differentiable in its interior, and $u'(t)\le\beta(t)u(t)$ there. For $t\in I$, $u(t)\le u(a)\exp(\int_a^t\beta(s)\,ds)$.
hypotheses: $I$ is an interval beginning at $a$, $u,\beta$ are continuous on $I$, $u$ is differentiable in its interior, and $u'(t)\le\beta(t)u(t)$ there.
conclusions: For $t\in I$, $u(t)\le u(a)\exp(\int_a^t\beta(s)\,ds)$.
